title: Send Your Name to Titan on NASA's Dragonfly Mission
summary:
We may still be some time away from sending humans to the distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission.

NASA is asking the public to send their names to Titan for an ambitious mission that will see a flying craft explore the Saturn moon in 2034, if all goes according to plan. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be placed on a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before January 15, 2027.

Dragonfly is an SUV-sized, nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch toward Titan in 2028. The agency says the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to fly between areas miles apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote on the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life."

Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world. The first was NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter, which arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 before its blades were damaged during a landing on January 18, 2024.

Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan. That would be Huygens, which operated for just a few hours on January 14, 2005, after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and it measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface. For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017, providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above.

Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk. "Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added. "Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments." Dragonfly's goals include learning more about prebiotic chemistry, the conditions before life arises in a location, and figuring out if Titan had habitable conditions in the past.
why_it_matters: Dragonfly will explore a distant world up close for years, and what it finds about the chemistry before life could change how we think about where life can begin.

background_read: Titan is the largest moon of Saturn and one of the most interesting worlds in the solar system, because it has a thick atmosphere and liquid on its surface, something no other moon is known to have.
A rotorcraft is a flying machine that uses spinning blades to lift off and land, which lets it visit many different places instead of staying in one spot.
Space agencies sometimes invite the public to send their names on a mission, placing them on a small chip carried by the spacecraft as a way of sharing the journey.

Dragonfly follows earlier visitors to Titan, including a lander that touched down there and an orbiter that flew past the moon many times, and it will study the moon's chemistry up close to learn about the conditions that could lead to life.
